title: “The River Can’t Be Trusted”
author: Cengiz Yar
content:
Peak tourist season had arrived in Ruidoso, New Mexico, and Mayor Lynn
Crawford was campaigning to convince the public that the village was safe. A
Republican with white hair and a Texas drawl, Crawford said he was frustrated
with residents who were sharing warnings of flooding on social media. “They
spout stuff off,” he said in a radio address on June 30, 2025. “And I don’t
know why they’re so afraid. I do not understand it.”

The community had experienced severe flooding the previous summer, after two
wildfires burned 25,000 acres above town, in the Sacramento Mountains. The
fires and floods had destroyed about 1,000 homes. Together, the Village of
Ruidoso and its smaller neighbor, Ruidoso Downs, are home to some 10,000
residents, but that number more than doubles during the summer.

Since then, residents had been on edge. A new monsoon season had arrived,
bringing sporadic flooding that jeopardized the town’s economic engine of
horse racing. At stake were big crowds to celebrate the Fourth of July, watch
quarter horse racing and enjoy cool weather that’d lured Texans here for
generations.

“We have flooding temporarily,” Crawford had told a Texas news anchor in an
interview. “And just almost as fast as it came to town, and went through town,
it’s gone.” Crawford, who is 64, managed an exclusive club at the Ruidoso
Downs Race Track & Casino and once called that his “real job.” He made less
than $26,000 as mayor.

But if the town’s economy was precarious, so was its geography. The South Fork
and Salt fires charred the landscape, leaving soils that didn’t easily absorb
water. Imagine spilling hot wax on a carpet, letting it cool and repeatedly
pouring water over it. Now place the wax on steep hills above a river lined
with log homes, tourist shops selling wooden bears and an iconic racetrack.

Officials were aware of the threat but clung to Ruidoso’s animating idea: that
nature could be subdued for the enjoyment of tourists and profit of the
community. Nowhere was this more apparent than at the track, where the Rio
Ruidoso, channeled through culverts, crossed the infield. After the 2024
flooding damaged the track, the culverts had been rebuilt with a $16 million
public investment authorized by New Mexico’s Democratic governor, Michelle
Lujan Grisham.

The track had only recently reopened, and flooding was again threatening to
derail the racing season. On June 26, internal records show, Ruidoso’s
emergency management department was at a heightened threat awareness level.
Flooding had destroyed a bridge upstream of the town, and the forecast called
for more rain.

But publicly, the village maintained it was prepared and the community was
safe. The next day, the emergency manager reduced the threat level a notch,
and the communications department chided residents for sharing warnings of
catastrophic flooding on social media, noting that some posts featured old
videos. “Protect our community from fear-based falsehoods,” the village
implored in a public service announcement.

![A man with white hair and a white beard sits at an office desk in front of
an American flag and village logo, resting his arm on his chair while looking
toward the camera.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/10/mobile2026-CengizYar-
Ruidoso-2_maxHeight_3000_maxWidth_3000-copy.jpg?w=752)Village of Ruidoso Mayor
Lynn Crawford, shown in his office, was presiding at a council meeting when
the flood hit.

On July 4, and one state over, [violent
flooding](https://www.texastribune.org/2026/05/06/texas-legislature-flood-
protection-bills-failed-july-4/) killed more than 130 people in central Texas.
But multiple tourists who were arriving in Ruidoso said they had no idea the
town was in danger. At the racetrack, the horses ran, and Crawford hosted
members at the Ruidoso Jockey Club, where private tables cost as much as six
figures.

That weekend, Sebastian Trotter and his family traveled to Ruidoso from El
Paso, Texas. Trotter was an Army helicopter pilot stationed at Fort Bliss; his
wife, Stephanie, was a nursing student. They thought the place looked family
friendly; they saw no warnings online. They brought their two children and
three dogs. On Sunday, July 6, they parked their trailer in a desirable spot
on the water’s edge at the Riverview RV Park. In online photos, the river
appeared gentle. “You could go put your toes in,” said Sebastian.

That day, the Rio Ruidoso — “noisy river,” in Spanish — briefly flooded and
firefighters rescued at least four people. The Trotters saw the water rise,
but the campground host said it was a regular occurrence. Then the river
receded.

In the park, the Trotters’ children, Sebastian Rowan, 7, and Charlotte, 4,
biked under the tall pines. The boy was a soccer player who was enchanted by
the idea of camping in the woods; Charlotte was bright and cheery, sometimes
applying glitter to her father’s mustache. Later, the family walked through
the village, where elk and wild horses occasionally graze near tourists.

On Tuesday, July 8, the Trotters were visiting a lake when they saw clouds
form. They decided to head into town, ordering pizza before allowing the
children to pick out souvenirs. The younger Sebastian selected a rainbow
gemstone, Charlotte a bracelet and a ring. Then they returned to the RV park,
where they relaxed by the river.

At 1 p.m., Crawford presided over a council meeting at Village Hall. He began
by recognizing the Texas flood victims and nodding to Ruidoso’s relative
success. “We want to keep all of central Texas in our thoughts and prayers and
see how bad it was and how fortunate we’ve been,” he said. “The goal of the
village is to protect the village.” That meant balancing public safety with
tourism, he said.

### Read More

[ ![](https://www.propublica.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/2026-CengizYar-
Ruidoso2-4_preview_maxWidth_3000_maxHeight_3000_ppi_72_embedColorProfile_true_quality_95.jpg?w=459&h=306&crop=1)
**Town Leaders Said They Were Prepared for Floods. First Responders
Disagree.** ](https://www.propublica.org/article/ruidoso-flood-emergency-
response-water-rescue)

At almost the same moment, storm clouds gathered in the mountains. Even short
periods of moderate rain on severe burn scars can unleash post-fire floods. By
1:30 p.m., radar indicated storms might douse both scars simultaneously. A
little before 2 p.m., firefighters texted images of the radar to one another.
“It could be interesting,” wrote one. [Only about a third of the department
was on duty at the time](https://www.propublica.org/article/ruidoso-flood-
emergency-response-water-rescue) and the chief, Cade Hall, had for weeks
declined to preposition additional flood specialists near low-lying areas.

Hall disputed ProPublica’s reporting about the emergency response but declined
to comment with specifics.

Less than an hour later, another flood arrived, carrying debris that backed up
behind bridges. The water kept coming, fanning onto roads until the normal
course of the river disappeared. What the wall of brown water carried told
residents it was time to panic.

Jason Fulcher, an owner of the Riverview RV Park, saw a tree-size log in the
waterway. Two miles downstream, a maintenance worker at a mobile home park saw
a car float past and lodge against a bridge.

Farther downstream, the track’s executives did not need physical signs of
danger; they knew what was coming because they’d been alerted.

But the Trotters were caught unprepared. Around 3 p.m., they retreated to
their trailer to escape the rain. Then the flood tore through a wall and took
their children.

![An SUV marked with an orange X and RV trailers sit stranded in mud and
debris following severe flash flooding in a wooded
area.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/2026-CengizYar-
Ruidoso-3_preview_maxWidth_3000_maxHeight_3000_ppi_72_embedColorProfile_true_quality_95.jpg?w=2560)The
July 2025 flood left Riverview RV Park, where the Trotter family and others
were staying, littered with debris.

* * *

The wildfire crisis engulfing the West presents a secondary threat that has
received less attention: Entire neighborhoods could wash away in debris flows
and floods that often follow.

Scientists say there’s a direct correlation between fire intensity and flood
risk. Research shows that if more than 20% of the ground burns at moderate to
high severity, especially on steep slopes, there’s an increased danger of
debris flows and post-fire flooding during storms. The fires that burned above
the Rio Ruidoso watershed far exceeded that threshold.

Before the 2025 tourist season, local and state officials had an opportunity
to safeguard Ruidoso and adapt to the realities of a warming climate that is
exacerbating wildfires and flooding. The state and village each commissioned
experts to model flooding scenarios. The engineers’ reports predicted serious
flooding. “They told us exactly where it was going to come and what it was
going to do,” said Hall, the fire chief. Federal emergency officials suggested
that significant parts of the town should relocate away from the river.

Instead, leaders from the mayor to the governor recommitted to tourism and the
racetrack.

### Ruidoso Is Surrounded on Three Sides by Thousands of Acres of Burn Scars

![](https://www.propublica.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/20261020-ruidoso-
locator_xs.jpg?w=752)The South Fork and Salt fires burned in 2024. The McBride
Fire was in 2022. Lucas Waldron/ProPublica

Since the July 8, 2025, flood, officials have insisted they performed
admirably against a historic disaster. Michael Martinez, the village’s former
deputy manager, who helped direct the response, said, “We’re lucky we didn’t
have a Texas.”

But according to five first responders, the tragedy could have been avoided.
All of the first responders spoke on the condition of anonymity for fear of
reprisal. Their accounts are supported by public records, including emails,
internal reports and hydrologic assessments. Before July 8, Crawford, Hall and
others made decisions that left residents and tourists vulnerable, even though
they knew a damaging flood was likely, first responders and officials say.

Some of those choices, such as the village’s promotion of tourism to visitors
largely unaware of the threat, appeared to be financially motivated, according
to current and former officials who worked on flood response. “Money was the
driver,” said Thora Walsh Padilla, the former president of the Mescalero
Apache Tribe, which is based south and west of town. “You’re taking a chance
with people who aren’t even from this area and don’t know how to get around
enough.” She added, “You’re putting them in jeopardy.”

Other missteps were caused by inaction: the failure to relocate vulnerable
residents and to replace infrastructure damaged during previous flooding, even
as the governor drove the state’s $16 million investment in the track. And
just before the flood arrived, at least one of the RV park’s owners received
emergency alerts but did not evacuate campers.

Village officials including Crawford did not respond to more than 70 questions
from ProPublica, including about whether they had emphasized tourism at the
track over public safety. But in an interview last year, Crawford said: “Who’s
to blame? I didn’t start the fire.”

Reached by phone, Kerry Gladden, the village’s public information officer,
referred questions to an attorney, who did not answer them. Village officials
have said that their emergency department sent text-message warnings before
the flood through a system that the public had to sign up for.

A spokesperson for Lujan Grisham said the state’s investments in the track
were necessary to protect life and safety. The track’s general manager, Rick
Baugh, did not respond to multiple inquiries about ProPublica’s reporting, and
one of the racing operation’s owners didn’t answer questions sent by email.

The lapses and missed opportunities in Ruidoso offer challenging lessons about
the harsh reality facing communities throughout the American West. This
summer, post-fire flooding and debris flows killed one person and prompted
more than a dozen rescues in Colorado. In August, flash floods in the Grand
Canyon killed three; some of those floodwaters had coursed over burned areas.
And in Utah, Gov. Spencer Cox declared a state of emergency following post-
fire flooding in three counties.

The West is not yet prepared for the spreading threat. While federal
scientists have created a [national model](https://www.usgs.gov/data/post-
wildfire-debris-flow-runout-hazard-assessment-pwfdf-r-collection-
updated-20260423) to assess the likelihood of post-fire debris flows,
communities don’t have an easily accessible tool to gauge their risk of post-
fire flooding.  

Ruidoso still looks like a tourist hub, but it survives on disaster aid from
the state and federal governments. Since 2024, the state and federal
governments have spent over half a billion dollars on disasters in Ruidoso —
nine times the village’s annual budget.

Even as funding pours in, first responders say the village remains
inadequately prepared to protect residents and tourists.

![Pedestrians stand near a street corner in downtown Ruidoso, across from a
large adobe wall featuring a welcome mural painted with the town's name and
Sierra Blanca peak.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/10/2026-CengizYar-
Ruidoso-4_preview_maxWidth_3000_maxHeight_3000_ppi_72_embedColorProfile_true_quality_95.jpg?w=1149)Ruidoso’s
bustling downtown on a Friday afternoon this past summer. The village and its
smaller neighbor, Ruidoso Downs, are home to some 10,000 residents, but that
number more than doubles during the summer.

* * *

Ruidoso is not a glitzy escape of vast alpine vistas. Homes are close
together, built into riverbanks and overhung with trees. Cabins abut RV parks.
Located in Lincoln County, it has long been an escape for working families
from Texas and soldiers stationed at Fort Bliss, 130 miles to the south. “Our
kids deserved this small trip,” Stephanie Trotter wrote on social media after
the July 8 flood.

The place they booked sat across from a 19th-century mill that’s recognized as
the village’s birthplace. One of the RV park’s owners, Fulcher, said that if
you looked hard enough, you might find bullet holes in the trees from old
Western battles.

The village’s colonial founders were unwise to set their community on the
river. The Mescalero Apache traditionally lived on hills above the creeks and
wetlands to avoid rising water and mosquitoes, Walsh Padilla said. Over and
over, the river flooded, including in 2008 and 2022. Randall Camp, the former
Lincoln County manager and public works director for Ruidoso, said, “The river
can’t be trusted.”

Many new residents did not understand the danger. Fulcher and his wife,
Lindsey, moved to Ruidoso from the Houston area in 2022, seeking a quiet life
near family. Jason was leaving a high-income, high-stress career in gas sales.
The 1.5 acre property they purchased sat just below confluences of the Rio
Ruidoso and two tributaries. Lindsey’s sister and brother-in-law had their own
RV park upriver.

The Fulchers arrived as the threat reached a new extreme. A decade ago,
researchers from Northern Arizona University studied tree rings on the
Mescalero Apache reservation, finding that fires had occurred regularly —
every six to 18 years, in many cases — until the turn of the 20th century.
Then they declined in frequency as the government started suppressing fires.
With fewer fires, the forests grew thick. The shade drew tourists. But, Walsh
Padilla said: “This isn’t natural. It’s not natural anymore.”

The Forest Service’s policy of quickly extinguishing fires was symbolically
tied to Lincoln County, where in 1950, firefighters found a singed bear cub in
the mountains northeast of Ruidoso. The injured cub was named Smokey and flown
to the National Zoo in Washington, D.C., where it became the living icon for
the agency’s ongoing messaging campaign.

As the climate warmed, the government’s policy of putting out fires
fundamentally altered the landscape. Between 1950 and 2010, wildfires in the
Rio Ruidoso watershed burned just under 11,000 acres, according to a
ProPublica analysis of data from the National Interagency Fire Center. Since
then, nearly 54,000 acres have burned — an area nearly five times larger than
in the previous 60 years. And scientists say those fires are hotter than ever,
as heavy fuels like Douglas firs and ponderosa pines lose moisture in the
warming climate.

In June 2024, two major fires ignited, and monsoon rains soon followed. A
16-foot flood tore through town on July 20, 2024.

![An aerial view reveals a charred hillside covered with burned, leafless
trees and patches of green regrowth following a forest
fire.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/10/mobile2026-CengizYar-
Ruidoso-5_maxHeight_3000_maxWidth_3000-copy.jpg?w=752)Three massive wildfires
have charred the mountains above Ruidoso since 2022.

The Fulchers’ house, which was located in their park, sustained minor damage,
but their relatives’ property, a couple hundred yards upstream, was destroyed.
The Federal Emergency Management Agency deemed Chelsey Jarvis and Darrel
McKay’s house uninhabitable and prohibited them from building even temporary
housing on the land. The couple closed the park for the season. “I wasn’t
going to put people in harm’s way because I wanted their money,” Jarvis said
during an October 2024 village meeting, as she begged the council to buy their
property. “It’s just going to be Groundhog Day. Next year it’s going to wash
away.”

Jarvis proposed they turn the park into a retention pond to slow floodwaters
and protect downstream businesses. Officials were considering such drastic
measures. The Natural Resources Conservation Service, a subagency of the U.S.
Department of Agriculture, had raised the idea of a large-scale buyout. It had
recently committed $106 million to move more than 600 homes following 2022
flooding in Kentucky.

The project in Ruidoso would be even more costly. Martinez, the village’s
former deputy manager, and Camp, who was then the county manager, estimated
they needed $650 million to move about 1,000 properties. But the NRCS would
only pay if a local partner provided a 25% match, meaning the county, village
or state would have to raise vast sums. While Jarvis and McKay immediately
said they wanted a buyout, Jason Fulcher was torn. He loved his property. But
he and his wife worried that the village’s infrastructure didn’t adequately
protect their home. In December 2024, they submitted a form saying they wanted
to be relocated.

During New Mexico’s 2025 legislative session, no lawmaker proposed funding a
buyout for Ruidoso. By spring, with the opportunity fading for a mass
relocation of homes and businesses, optimism crept back into public discourse.

According to Jarvis and McKay, Crawford encouraged them to reopen their park,
saying the village needed affordable rentals. (Neither Crawford nor the
village answered a question about the interaction.) As tourist season
approached, the families adopted different strategies. Jarvis said she was
never comfortable with reopening, but McKay felt the family had little choice
given how much they’d invested. They resolved to keep their property open but
only to book half the camp sites.

Fulcher, on the other hand, wanted a full park from June to September, when
the most tourists arrived and so did the monsoons. He said he’d withdrawn all
his retirement savings to cover the down payment and improvements on the
$645,000 property, and he was so attached to the place that he’d rebuffed
multiple potential buyers. The park needed to be fully operational, he said,
“because at 50% operational, we’re losing money every month.”

On March 31, 2025, the village released a new map of the floodplain online,
which allowed viewers to zoom in on their properties. The map was based on
flood models created by a company called Cobb, Fendley & Associates, which had
months earlier outlined a dire scenario to village officials.

### The Trotter Family’s Campsite Sat on the Edge of the River

The Village of Ruidoso’s floodplain and floodway maps show that most of the RV
park was at risk prior to the July 2025 flood.

![](https://www.propublica.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/20261020-riverview-
floodplain_xs.jpg?w=752)The floodway is the river channel where fast-moving
water flows during a flood. A floodplain is the area expected to flood during
a 100-year storm. Sources: Satellite image via NAIP. 2025 floodplain and
floodway data were obtained from the Village of Ruidoso. Lucas
Waldron/ProPublica

The company had been hired to model what might happen in a 100-year storm — a
term that reflects the anticipated depth and intensity of rainfall. In January
2025, a Cobb Fendley engineer sent an email to the village saying that the
company thought a 100-year storm would bring six times the volume of the July
2024 flood that destroyed Jarvis and McKay’s home. In a separate report, Cobb
Fendley identified more than 200 at-risk addresses. The list included their
property, as well as the Fulchers’ RV park.

But the village didn’t make clear the threat to existing properties. When
officials discussed the map, they often focused on its impact on development
and building permits. “There was never a time where we specifically said,
‘Someone can die,’” Martinez, the village’s former deputy manager, said in an
interview. “Never have I ever stated those words. Everything I’ve ever shared
with somebody has been: ‘This is the floodplain. This is what was adopted.
These are the new high-water marks. If we ever get a flood that is a 100-year
flood, the waters will get this high.’”

Both RV parks were in the floodplain. But both Fulcher and McKay said they’d
internalized the government’s optimism. “The leadership dang sure makes you
feel like it’s gonna be OK,” said McKay. “All they kept saying was build back
better. We’re stronger.”

![National Guard service members load white sandbags from wooden pallets into
the open trunk of an SUV ahead of flood
preparations.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/10/mobile2026-CengizYar-
Ruidoso-6_maxHeight_3000_maxWidth_3000-copy.jpg?w=752)Members of the New
Mexico National Guard provided sandbags in order to help local residents
protect against flooding last summer. ![An elevated view shows a mud-caked,
flooded horse-racing track surrounded by standing water and mountain ridges
under a cloudy sky.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/10/2026-CengizYar-
Ruidoso-7_preview_maxWidth_3000_maxHeight_3000_ppi_72_embedColorProfile_true_quality_95.jpg?w=1149)The
destroyed Ruidoso Downs racetrack on July 31, 2025. Continued flooding left it
caked in mud and debris.

* * *

On May 25, 2025, Lujan Grisham celebrated the reopening of the track, aided by
the funds she secured. “Ruidoso Downs has reopened for its first races since
those disasters in record time,” read a post on the governor’s official
Instagram page. “Ruidoso Strong!”

New Mexico’s constitution prohibits the use of public funds on private
businesses in most cases, but there are exceptions for certain public and
economic development projects. Records show that starting in September 2024,
New Mexico’s then-transportation secretary, Ricky Serna, directed a team of
engineers to prioritize work at the track, even as his subordinates raised
concerns that FEMA might not reimburse the costs because the project hadn’t
yet met the agency’s standards.

Crews excavated an 8-acre basin in the infield to serve as a holding pond,
while contractors rebuilt the culverts under the track and reinforced the road
leading into it. These efforts were designed to slow floodwater, but the
project also allowed the track to reopen.

The track was best known for hosting the world’s richest quarter horse race,
the All American Futurity, which awarded $3 million annually, with half going
to the contest’s winner.

Horses at the track were cared for by grooms, many of whom were immigrants.
The grooms worked for horse trainers rather than the track itself. But the
track provided space for them to sleep in barns and storage rooms, in what one
executive called industry-standard conditions. Baugh, the general manager, did
not answer questions about living conditions at the track. Izzy Trejo,
executive director of the New Mexico Racing Commission, said in an email that
the commission had no authority over the matter. “The living conditions for
the grooms is the responsibility of each individual trainer,” said Trejo.

But there was little scrutiny of such issues at “our beloved racetrack,” as
Crawford has called it. In addition to the mayor, the village’s public
information officer previously handled publicity for the track and the mayor
of Ruidoso Downs previously oversaw its security.

The racetrack’s various businesses and their owners, Jana and Johnny Trotter —
they are not related to Sebastian and Stephanie — contributed more than
$35,000 to Lujan Grisham’s gubernatorial campaigns. Michael Coleman, a
spokesperson for the governor, said in an email, “The infrastructure
improvement projects at Ruidoso Downs and the surrounding area were undertaken
because of the life-safety risk the site posed to the surrounding community.”
Coleman said the project was “not solely for economic development reasons.”

But the track framed the project differently. “The clock’s ticking,” said Tim
Keithley, the track’s former marketing director, in a February
[report](https://www.krqe.com/news/new-mexico/ruidoso-downs-race-track-
working-around-the-clock-to-repair-damage-from-summer-flooding/) by KRQE, a
New Mexico outlet. “We need to race so that the community can have tourism and
bring those Texans over to spend some money with us.”

As work at the track progressed, one urgent mitigation project upriver lagged.
Officials were concerned about old and damaged bridges and culverts on the Rio
Ruidoso. During floods they could act like dams, forcing rising water onto
roads and increasing the threat downstream. “If you have a bunch of debris
that comes in and clogs bridges, at some point that’s going to release,” said
Eric Queller, Ruidoso’s emergency manager.

In the year leading up to the 2025 tourist season, bridge repairs and
replacements once again fell by the wayside as village and state officials
argued over who was responsible for them. The work at the track, meanwhile,
was completed by Memorial Day.

On Sunday, July 6, when firefighters made at least four flooding rescues, the
Ruidoso News posted a video about the track repair on its Facebook page. In
the video, which was produced by the newspaper’s general manager, Eugene
Heathman, Crawford said the infrastructure was holding.

The next day, an executive at the paper’s parent company, El Rito Media, told
Heathman his journalism, which had included footage of severe flood damage,
was bad for business. The executive has since left the company and told
ProPublica he was acting on the orders of El Rito’s publisher, Richard Connor.
In a statement, Connor denied attempting to influence coverage. “We have dug,
investigated, and sought out all angles in our flood and racetrack coverage,”
he said.

Heathman soon resigned. The video of Crawford at the track has disappeared
from the internet, and Heathman’s footage showing flood damage has been
removed from the Ruidoso News’ Facebook account.

The Rio Ruidoso near downtown Ruidoso rose quickly during a flash flood on
July 30, 2025, after rain hit burn scar on the surrounding mountains.

* * *

Just before 2 p.m. on July 8, a fierce rain began to fall near the headwaters
of one of the Rio Ruidoso’s upper forks. Within 10 minutes, nearly three-
quarters of an inch of rain pelted the charred ground. At 2:12 p.m., the
National Weather Service sent out a flash flood warning, which it upgraded to
an emergency 35 minutes later, after debris slid down steep slopes and into
the river.

At Village Hall, Crawford adjourned the council meeting just before 3:10 p.m.,
saying: “We’ve had a wall of water come over. It’s predicted this is the big
one.” Shortly after, he called the track’s general manager, Rick Baugh.  

Josh Gibson, a track executive, was with Baugh when the call arrived. He said
Crawford “told him he had 45 minutes or so before the water got there.” (Baugh
did not respond to repeated inquiries, and Crawford and Gladden, the public
information officer, did not answer a question about the call.)

The advance notice allowed Baugh and his colleagues to alert dozens of grooms
living in the barns to evacuate before the flood reached them.

Three miles upstream, at the Riverview RV Park, Jason Fulcher, the Trotters
and other campers stood by the river. They talked about the weather. They
talked about which trailers they preferred. They talked about whether there
were any reports of ghosts in the area. The Trotters’ children played in the
shade.

Multiple people who were in the park received text alerts warning of flooding.
But all of them, including one of the park’s owners, said the alerts seemed
routine. “We received watch and warning alerts daily, sometimes multiple times
in the same day,” Fulcher said in an email. He also told ProPublica in an
interview that he’d followed the village’s advice: “Just be vigilant. Watch
the skies, stay out of low-lying areas, watch the river.” But he didn’t stay
out of low-lying areas, because his property sat in one.

The Trotters said that although their phones were on, they didn’t receive any
alerts from the National Weather Service. They did not know about the
village’s alerts. “There was nothing,” Sebastian said.

Residents had “alert fatigue.” So officials wanted first responders to drive
into threatened areas on dangerous flood days to ensure that people evacuated.
In parts of the community, including much of Ruidoso Downs, first responders
showed up with loudspeakers, telling people to seek high ground just before
the flood arrived.

But at the Riverview RV Park, no one came, even though the park sat just about
a third of a mile from the fire department’s headquarters.

After receiving the alerts, Fulcher began his monsoon season routine: He went
to the riverbank to ask guests to move back. Fulcher said the Trotters were
among those he asked to step slightly away from the river; the Trotters
dispute this.

When it started to rain, the children retreated to their trailer, which had an
extending compartment known as a slide-out. The river rose, carrying branches
and rocks. The Trotters joined the kids, preparing to drive to higher ground.
Then they heard a noise that Sebastian likened to television static through
noise canceling headphones.

According to the Trotters, the trailer door was open and blocked by debris.
Sebastian stuck his leg out and was temporarily caught, but he managed to get
back inside. He was reaching for a mattress when the flood ripped off the
slide-out. Stephanie, holding both children, was sucked into the water. “Once
I was in the water, I only had Charlotte in my arms,” she said. Sebastian dove
in after his son.

Fulcher had steered out of the park in a truck. At the road he was met by
brown, sediment-laden floodwaters carrying vehicles and a dumpster. The flood
was remarkable for both its scale — a river gauge showed twice the volume of
the July 2024 flood — and its bulk. One survivor said it felt like liquid
cement. Fulcher left his truck and sprinted to a high point from which he
could see his house. His two children were trapped inside. He stepped onto a
building, planning to swim to them, but the structure collapsed. Fulcher
climbed a wall and tried to swim but was pushed back. In the house, his
children clung to a ceiling fan as rising water pushed their mattress toward
the ceiling.

![Smudges and dirt marks appear on a white ceiling next to a fan blade, above
a wall featuring a painted daisy decoration.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/10/Handprint2_maxHeight_3000_maxWidth_3000-2.jpg?w=527)Muddy
handprints were left on the ceiling in the house of Jason and Lindsey Fulcher,
owners of the Riverview RV Park. Obtained by ProPublica

The campground host, Jere Stark, had made his way to a pavilion, where he used
a post to shield his body from the water. Stark, who is 71, was trying to help
another camper, Benjamin Timothy Feagin, from the bed of a truck. The flood
pulled them in.

Near their camp site, the younger Sebastian held onto a tree. His father
repeatedly tried to reach him but struggled to move in the water. He was hit
by a boulder and a floating truck, he said. The boy could not hold on any
longer and lost his grip.

By about 3:30 p.m., there were at least eight firefighters at Riverview,
including two swiftwater technicians in a vehicle capable of navigating
floodwaters. Across the waterway, they saw a man 20 feet up a tree. The elder
Sebastian Trotter was in the water below him, grabbing a tree trunk, wounded
and barely able to speak.

The two swiftwater technicians waded to the Fulchers’ house and retrieved the
Fulcher children, who were huddled together on the mattress.

There were still more children to rescue, but not all the first responders
knew that.

The Trotters had been separated. Firefighters found the older Sebastian alone.
A few hundred yards downstream, first responders helped rescue Stephanie
Trotter and Stark. Stephanie said she’d been with her daughter, but the girl
was now gone.

Later, when the water receded, Fulcher and McKay pried open the Trotters’
crumpled trailer. Inside, they found the Trotters’ surviving dog.

The first body was found under a bridge around 5:20 p.m. It was Feagin, who
had been in the pavilion with Stark.

Firefighters split up to scour the riverside for the children. One group
walked downstream. It passed Paradise Canyon, where Stephanie Trotter had been
rescued, searching the corners of the floodplain where waters had receded.

Another group moved upriver. The light faded, trees casting long shadows.
“Couldn’t see much,” said a firefighter. “Everything’s different and washed
out, and all you could see was really the little spotlight on your
flashlight.” He came to a softball field full of scattered furniture. He
passed a bridge and paused. “I looked back. Something told me, ‘Look back.’”

He saw the shape of a child’s body. It was Sebastian Rowan Trotter.
Charlotte’s body had been found not far away.

![A narrow, concrete beam bridge spans a shallow, muddy stream flanked by
dense green trees and dirt banks.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/10/mobile2026-CengizYar-
Ruidoso-8_maxHeight_3000_maxWidth_3000-copy.jpg?w=752)The body of Benjamin
Timothy Feagin was found under a bridge on Friedenbloom Drive.

* * *

In their private correspondence on July 8 and 9, state officials said they
were worried about the racetrack. While firefighters were searching for the
Trotters’ children, a senior disaster recovery official named Jeremy Klass
sent a message asking if horses needed evacuation. They didn’t.

The next morning, an official notified Klass and other colleagues about the
racetrack. “Village is concerned,” he wrote.

“This should be a priority,” responded Heath Dobrovolny, the state floodplain
coordinator.

Dobrovolny said he didn’t recall the text exchange, but he was likely focused
on preventing casualties downstream from the track. He also disputed that, as
state floodplain coordinator, he had favored the track over the village.
Regina Chacon, the New Mexico Department of Homeland Security and Emergency
Management’s deputy cabinet secretary, said in an email that the agency was
concerned that debris buildup “would apply pressure on the dam between the
infield” and a downstream community.

At a news conference on the morning of July 9, Crawford repeatedly noted how
high the water had crested: “This is historic.” Since then, officials have
said they did everything in their power to protect the village.

“We pretty much did everything we possibly could and everything worked out, I
guess, as best it could for the situation that we had,” Hall, Ruidoso’s fire
chief, said. “I don’t know that I would have done anything differently.”

“Will I tell you it’s successful when we lost three lives? No,” said Ali Rye,
the state homeland security director. But, she said, “We put out every bit of
messaging we possibly could. I don’t know, from the state’s perspective, what
more we could have done.”

![A man with short graying hair sits in an auditorium chair with his legs
crossed, looking off to the side.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/10/2026-CengizYar-
Ruidoso-9_preview_maxWidth_3000_maxHeight_3000_ppi_72_embedColorProfile_true_quality_95.jpg?w=527)Heath
Dobrovolny, the state floodplain coordinator at the time of the flood last
year, now serves as Ruidoso’s deputy village manager.

And a month after the flood, in a video interview published by a horse racing
website, Lujan Grisham said, “No governor, no state, no president, no one at
the federal level can sort of predict what happens with the weather and
emergencies.”

In truth, the disaster had been all but predicted in the reports created for
the state and village. “Unfortunately, it’s stuff that was modeled,” said
Joseph Loverich, a civil engineer with the firm JE Fuller, which in 2024
created multiple flood models for the state. And Cobb Fendley’s model had told
the village that even worse flooding could be coming. The July 8 flood carried
a third of the volume the company anticipated for a 100-year flood. (Cobb
Fendley did not respond to detailed questions about how it arrived at its
conclusions.)

On Oct. 8, three months after the flood, Lincoln County held another meeting
about a potential buyout for property owners at risk. Martinez, Ruidoso’s
deputy village manager, said: “That wasn’t even a big one. I mean, that was
half of what we expected, of the max.” July 8 had been a 50-year flood, he
said. “It could be twice as much. That’s the honest-to-God truth.”

“So you guys knew?” interjected Fulcher.

“We had campers,” said Jarvis.

Lincoln County’s new manager, Jason Burns, cut her off: “Hold on. Listen to
us. That’s not what he’s saying.”

Within weeks, Martinez adjusted his language. In an interview on Oct. 21, he
said: “Did I do enough? I ask myself that question every day, and I come to
the same realization every day: I don’t know what more I could have done. I
honestly don’t.”

Months later, he left Ruidoso for a job in El Paso. He was soon replaced by
Dobrovolny, the former state floodplain coordinator who had helped direct work
at the track. In July, Dobrovolny emailed village employees, emphasizing a
policy prohibiting them from talking to journalists. A video of the
contentious October meeting originally posted by the county has been removed
from the internet. In an email, Burns said the video’s disappearance was “not
intentional.”

![A portrait of a woman looking thoughtfully out a window while a man with a
mustache stands in the background behind her.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/10/2026-CengizYar-
Ruidoso-10_preview_maxWidth_3000_maxHeight_3000_ppi_72_embedColorProfile_true_quality_95.jpg?w=752)Stephanie
and Sebastian Trotter live in El Paso, Texas, a two-and-a-half-hour drive from
Ruidoso, near a park the city named after their children.

* * *

The Trotters held a celebration of life for their children on Aug. 15.
Sebastian was still recovering from a broken bone in a foot, nerve damage in
his legs, and wounds on his legs and arms. Tattoos on his forearms had been
partially removed due to the injuries.

A few weeks later, the All American Futurity was held in Albuquerque for a
second consecutive season. In Ruidoso, Crawford arranged a viewing party at
the Jockey Club. When a bank of televisions showed horses bursting through the
starting gate, feet stomped on the club’s carpet. The track outside was empty
and quiet. Still, multiple people in the club said they anticipated racing
would return. A woman from Texas named Dusty Milanes said the dangers in
Ruidoso were being overblown. “There’s parts of the community that are totally
normal,” said Milanes, who wore pink cowboy boots. Asked where that was, she
said, “High ground.”

The Jockey Club was surviving on restaurant sales and catering contracts, and
Crawford had to lay off most of his employees. In private, state officials
discussed distancing themselves from their $16 million rehabilitation effort
at the track. “We have to keep in mind and project to the public NMDOT had
minimal involvement in this,” a district engineer for the Department of
Transportation wrote in an email in August 2025.

![The sun sets behind distant mountain peaks over a field of tall grass,
wildflowers and scattered silhouetted burned
trees.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/10/mobile2026-CengizYar-
Ruidoso-11_maxHeight_3000_maxWidth_3000-copy.jpg?w=752)New growth covers
sections of burn scar above Ruidoso this summer.

* * *

By spring, green shoots sprouted on the hills above the Rio Ruidoso. New
growth on burn scars can slow the worst effects of flooding, but scientists
say it’s important to not become complacent. “This is not a one-and-done kind
of thing,” said Belize Lane, an associate professor of civil and environmental
engineering at Utah State University. “There is still an opportunity for many,
many more events that may not look like that, but may still be hugely
destructive.”

But in Ruidoso, people started to say that the worst had passed. “Everybody
always goes back to sleep,” said Camp, the former county manager.

In July, the Ruidoso News published a story about the village government’s
performance during the flooding, which largely relied on the mayor’s analysis.
“The legacy is one of resilience, not giving up, fortitude, rugged
individualism, the ability for you to be all you can be and not give up,” said
Crawford.

The track was closed, and weeds soon grew 6 feet high in the holding pond. The
All American Futurity was moved to Texas. Still, the Jockey Club continued to
collect dues from members and Crawford promised that hooves would again
thunder in Ruidoso. “The track deal isn’t over yet,” he said during a council
meeting.

The Fulchers mostly avoided their old RV park. The state had finally secured
$249 million for a buyout program, with more than three-quarters of the funds
coming from the federal government. But the Fulchers, who now run a mountain-
man themed store, selling antlers and rifles, hadn’t yet received an appraisal
for their property.

They had settled a wrongful death lawsuit brought by the Trotters and Feagin’s
family, with an insurance company paying an undisclosed amount.
“Accountability is at the forefront of my mind,” Sebastian said during a March
television interview. He said he would not “just let us be forgotten — let our
kids be forgotten.” An attorney for the Trotters also sent the village a
letter notifying officials that they intended to sue.

Crawford said that he anticipated the Trotters would sue but declined to
discuss potential litigation.

![A wooden cross decorated with flowers stands attached to a tree in front of
a collapsed building in a wooded area.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/10/mobile2026-CengizYar-
Ruidoso-12_maxHeight_3000_maxWidth_3000-copy.jpg?w=752)A small memorial for
the three lives lost in the flood now hangs at the Riverview RV Park.

The park now sat empty and taped off. The roof of the Fulchers’ house sagged,
and a child’s handprints were still visible on the ceiling.

Out front, on a towering tree, there was a white cross and, beneath it, a
plaque.

_In loving memory of Benjamin “Tim” Feagin,_  
_Sebastian Rowan Trotter,_  
_Charlotte Emery Trotter,_  
_And their two dogs Zeus & Ellie._

The Fulchers put the memorial up on the anniversary of the flood. A
firefighter who had helped find one of the Trotters’ children attended. “We
carry a lot of guilt for things that we weren’t able to do,” he said. “We feel
like we could have done more.”

The village continued to advertise tourism in West Texas. During the summer, a
digital billboard near the Trotters’ house flashed a Ruidoso promotion.
Sebastian saw it when he filled up on gas.

Just upstream of the closed race track, a mobile home park was mostly full.
Children played in the street, and occupied trailers sat above the river. The
park’s managers said they were following local rules. “I don’t think it’ll
ever flood again like that,” said one. The Rio Ruidoso babbled. It looked
welcoming. On a summer day, you could go put your toes in.
